claims.text: Controlled heat treatment can direct phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Tailored annealing temperature–time profiles and cooling rates modulate diffusional kinetics between competing FCC and BCC phases.
As-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs can have mixed, non-equilibrium microstructures containing precursor FCC and/or BCC regions.
Solution treatment, controlled annealing, and defined quenching or cooling can be used as a systematic phase-control procedure.
Selected annealing temperatures, durations, and cooling rates can permit significant but limited atomic diffusion.
Heat treatment changes the phase interfaces and precipitate/matrix morphology between FCC and BCC regions.
Heat treatment alters diffusion kinetics in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Heat treatment alters thermodynamic driving forces governing phase evolution.
Changes in diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces favor nucleation and growth of one phase or refinement of the FCC/BCC phase mixture.
The combination of temperature, time, and cooling shifts the free-energy balance between FCC and BCC phases.
Varying the heat-treatment regimen will systematically change phase fractions.
Varying the heat-treatment regimen may change grain or precipitate sizes.
Heat-treatment-induced changes in phase fractions and morphology can produce improved or tailored mechanical properties relative to a non-optimized baseline.
Conventional melting or powder metallurgy without optimized heat treatment can result in a less-controlled or heterogeneous microstructure.
Phase control requires enough diffusion to enable phase transformations.
Excessively aggressive heat treatment can cause undesirable coarsening or over-aging and thereby limit phase control.
XRD and electron microscopy can be used to quantify phase fractions and microstructural features in the treated alloys.
